summary: A catalogue of network training materials that Internet trainers could use to teach their users. It is an informational listing of resources, not a technical specification.

eli5.summary: It is a list of lesson books and slides for teachers who explain the internet to others.

questions: where to find network training resources
subtitle: A guide to quality network training materials for Internet educators and users.

tldr.problem: Internet trainers struggle to find and create quality training materials as more people need to learn network and Internet skills.
tldr.mechanism: A working group collected and catalogued existing training materials across multiple formats—guides, slides, workshops, online tutorials—and published them with metadata so trainers can find and reuse what exists rather than starting from scratch.
tldr.outcome: Trainers have access to a curated collection of resources covering Internet basics, web, email, security, and specialized topics, reducing duplication of effort and improving training consistency.

today: RFC 2007 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. The need for training materials remains relevant today, though the specific tools and platforms have evolved since 1996. The RFC provides historical insight into how the Internet community approached the challenge of scaling education as the network grew.

sections.title: The Training Materials Challenge
sections.content:
As the Internet expanded in the mid-1990s, demand for training grew rapidly. Librarians, computing center staff, and network support professionals all needed to teach users the basics and best practices of Internet use. However, each organization was creating its own materials, duplicating work and straining resources.

RFC 2007 addresses this by collecting and organizing existing training materials in one place. Produced by the TRAINMAT working group (a joint effort of the IETF and TERENA), it is an informational document that provides pointers to quality resources rather than prescribing how training should be done.
sections.eli5: Many teachers had to write lessons from scratch. This document says, "Here are the lessons that already exist. Use them instead of writing new ones."

sections.title: Types of Training Materials Included
sections.content:
The catalogue organizes materials into seven categories:

User Guides: Step-by-step manuals explaining Internet tools and services. Examples include the Internet Passport guide covering tools like FTP, email, the Web, and Gopher.

Resource Guides: Collections of pointers to useful online resources and services.

Trainer Guides: Materials designed specifically for educators teaching others.

Presentation Material: Slides, overhead transparencies, and speaker notes for lectures.

Workshop Exercises: Hands-on practice materials with detailed instructions.

Self-Paced Material: Online tutorials that learners can work through independently, such as the TONIC interactive tutorial.

Online Collections: Special curated collections of training resources assembled for shared use.
sections.eli5: The materials come in many forms: books to read, slides to show, exercises to try, and lessons online that you can learn at your own speed.

sections.title: Example Resources in the Catalogue
sections.content:
The RFC lists specific training materials available at the time of publication. Examples include:

The Internet Passport (667 pages), a comprehensive beginner's guide from NorthWestNet, covering Internet services, tools, and real-world uses in health care and education. The Net: User Guidelines and Netiquette, available in multiple languages, teaches responsible practice on email, FTP, and Usenet. Video resources like the Global Quest Video and The Video Guide to the Internet serve learners who prefer visual material. Online tutorials like TONIC (The Online Netskills Interactive Tutorial) allow self-paced learning. The catalogue includes over 30 entries, each with contact information, language, cost, and format details.
sections.eli5: For example, one guide teaches you how to use email and FTP safely and politely. Another is a video that shows you how the Internet works. Some are free, some cost money. Most are available online.

sections.title: A Living Document
sections.content:
The catalogue was designed to be a "living document"—not a static RFC published once and forgotten. The TRAINMAT working group maintained an online version at http://www.trainmat.ietf.org/ that could be updated as new materials were created or existing ones changed. Trainers could submit new resources via an HTML form, and an international editorial board reviewed additions before including them.

While RFC 2007 captures the state of available training materials in October 1996, the online version was expected to be more current. This hybrid approach—an RFC as a snapshot and a web version for updates—recognized that training materials evolve constantly as technology changes.
sections.eli5: The RFC is a snapshot from 1996, but the real list was kept online and updated as new training materials were created.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content:
By the mid-1990s, the rapid growth of the Internet user base created a critical need for quality education. Training materials are a public good: once created, they benefit many users and reduce redundant work. RFC 2007 standardized how these materials are catalogued (via the TRAINMAT template), making it easier for trainers to find, evaluate, and reuse existing work.

The document reflects the IETF's philosophy of sharing knowledge to accelerate Internet adoption and competence. Creating standards for how to document and share training materials supports the entire community, not just specialized implementers.
sections.eli5: Good training helps the Internet work better because users understand the rules and tools. By sharing training materials instead of each teacher making their own, everyone learns better and faster.

references.text: Postel, J. and J. Reynolds, "Instructions to RFC Authors", RFC 1543, October 1993.
